home.titolo: Traffic GA4 misses without cookie consent
home.descrizione: Estimate the sessions, conversions and revenue GA4 doesn’t show because cookie consent is missing, with their uncertainty. Your data stays in your browser.

strumento.descrizione: Upload a GA4 export, enter your banner’s consent rate and read the estimated totals of sessions, orders and revenue, each with its range of uncertainty.

guida.titolo: Guide: GA4 export and consent rate
guida.descrizione: How to create the GA4 exploration to upload, find the consent rate in your CMP, check whether GA4 is already estimating, and read the results.

metodo.descrizione: Where the numbers come from: what GA4 data is missing, which assumptions are needed about visitors who don’t accept, how the range is built, its limits.

validazione.descrizione: How the method was tested on synthetic data with a known answer: how often the range is right, and what a wrong assumption costs in each scenario.

privacy.descrizione: Your GA4 file is processed in your browser: no server, cookies, analytics or external resources. What happens to your data and how to check it yourself.

comeFatto.descrizione: Who made Uncounted, how it was built with Claude in phases approved by the author, how it was tested, and the limits of working this way.

avvio.titolo: How much traffic does GA4 miss?
avvio.sottotitolo: Three steps: the file, a check, your consent rate. Then the estimate.
avvio.poi2Testo: One to three questions, so that what Google already estimates isn’t counted twice.
avvio.poi3Testo: You’ll find it in the reports of your banner platform (CMP). Four short answers; “I don’t know” is allowed.

file.qualeFileTesto: A CSV exported from a GA4 free-form exploration, with “Date” and “Session default channel group” as rows and “Sessions”, “Total users”, “Key events”, “Transactions”, “Total revenue” as values. The last four are optional.
file.privacy: The file is read in this browser tab and isn’t sent to anyone.
file.quanteMancano: how many are missing: after your answers
file.colonnaEventi: Which key events column do you want to estimate?

erroreFile.file_vuoto_r: Export the exploration from GA4 again as CSV.
erroreFile.file_binario: The file doesn’t look like a text CSV (it may be an Excel or PDF file).
erroreFile.file_binario_r: In GA4, choose Export data → CSV.
erroreFile.solo_commenti: The file contains only comment lines.
erroreFile.solo_commenti_r: Check that the exploration has data in the selected date range and export it again.
erroreFile.colonna_mancante: Column {campo} is missing. In row {riga} I found: {trovate}.
erroreFile.colonna_mancante_r_dimensione: In the exploration, add the dimension {campo} to Rows and export again.
erroreFile.colonna_mancante_r_metrica: In the exploration, add the metric “Sessions” to Values and export again.
erroreFile.data_non_valida_r: The Date column must contain dates as YYYYMMDD (e.g. 20260315). Use the “Date” dimension, not “Week” or “Month”.
erroreFile.numero_non_valido_r: Check that the column holds a numeric metric and that the file wasn’t edited by hand. Both 1,234.56 and 1234.56 are accepted.
erroreFile.nessuna_riga: I didn’t find any data rows after the headers.
erroreFile.nessuna_riga_r: Check the exploration’s date range and that the Rows are “Date” and “Session default channel group”.
erroreFile.sessioni_zero_r: Check the exploration’s date range and filters.
erroreFile.altri_errori_r: Fix the first ones: they often have the same cause.

avvisoFile.utenti_attivi: The users column is “Active users”, not “Total users”: that’s fine, but the two numbers differ slightly.
avvisoFile.colonne_mancanti: Columns not found: {campi}. These won’t be estimated.
avvisoFile.numeri_misti: The file mixes number formats (1.234,56 and 1,234.56): each value was read on its own. Check the totals.
avvisoFile.duplicati: {n} rows had the same date and channel as another row: their values were added up. This happens when the exploration has an extra dimension in Rows.
avvisoFile.ambigui: {n} values such as “1.234” could be read two ways: they were read as thousands (1234). Check the totals.
avvisoFile.canale_not_set: Some rows have the channel “(not set)”: they are treated as a channel of their own.
avvisoFile.totaliDiversi: The rows don’t add up to the total row of the export: {elenco}. This usually happens when the exploration showed only some of the rows (“Show rows” below the maximum) or the file was edited. Check before trusting the estimate.
avvisoFile.totaliVoce: {m} {a} in the rows, {b} in the total

cm.titolo: Does your export already contain data estimated by Google?
cm.intro: If GA4 is already estimating traffic without consent, adding another estimate would count it twice.
cm.d1: How is Consent Mode set up on the site?
cm.d1Aiuto: In Basic, Google tags fire only after the visitor accepts. In Advanced they fire right away and, without consent, send cookieless pings. To check: open the site with Tag Assistant without accepting cookies; if you still see requests to Google Analytics, it’s Advanced.
cm.advancedNota: tags fire right away; one or two more questions
cm.nonsoNota: you can see the estimate, with a warning
cm.d2Aiuto: In GA4: Admin → Data display → Reporting identity.
cm.d3: What does the data quality icon in the exploration say?
cm.d3Aiuto: It’s the small icon at the top, next to the exploration’s title. Advanced isn’t enough: Google turns on modeling only above certain traffic thresholds (at least 1,000 events per day without consent for 7 days, and 1,000 users per day with consent on 7 of the previous 28 days), and not always.
cm.nonTrovo: I don’t know / I can’t find the icon
cm.esitoStima: You can estimate. The export contains only observed data.
cm.esitoIncerto: Use this estimate with caution. It holds only if the export doesn’t already contain data estimated by Google; otherwise traffic without consent would be counted twice.
cm.esitoBlocco: Your export already contains Google’s estimate of traffic without consent. Adding another one would count it twice, so the estimator stops here.
cm.esitoBloccoNota: The totals shown are those in your file, unchanged.
cm.riepBasic: Basic: the export contains only observed data
cm.riepAdvancedOsservata: Advanced, reporting identity not “Blended”: observed data only
cm.riepAdvancedNo: Advanced, Google’s modeling not active: observed data only
cm.riepIncerto: Not checked: use the estimate with caution
cm.confrontoTitolo: Optional: compare Google’s estimate with the estimator’s
cm.confrontoTesto: Temporarily set the reporting identity to “Device-based”, export the same exploration again and upload it here: it will contain only observed data. The setting applies to every user of the property until you change it back, so remember to switch to “Blended” again.
cm.tassoNonServe: Not needed: with Google’s modeling active there’s nothing to estimate. It becomes active again if you upload the second file for the comparison.

tasso.intro: You’ll find it in the reports of your banner platform (CMP): Cookiebot, iubenda, OneTrust, Usercentrics and similar.
tasso.valoreErrore: Enter a percentage between 1 and 99, for example 45 or 45%.
tasso.misura: How does your CMP calculate it?
tasso.misuraAiuto: It matters because a visitor who accepts and comes back ten times produces ten sessions in GA4 with a single consent.
tasso.ignora: Does the rate include visitors who make no choice?
tasso.ignoraAiuto: Visitors who leave or keep browsing without touching the banner haven’t given consent: for GA4 that’s the same as declining. Many CMPs calculate the rate only among visitors who clicked.
tasso.inclusoNota: visitors who ignore the banner count as “not accepted”
tasso.esclusoNota: it’s calculated only among visitors who clicked
tasso.quotaIgnora: Share of visitors who ignore the banner (%)
tasso.quotaIgnoraNota: If you leave it empty, about 15% is assumed, with a wide range (4% to 43%).
tasso.riepDevice: derived from the rates by device
tasso.riepIgnoraIncluso: visitors who ignore the banner are included
tasso.riepIgnoraEscluso: visitors who ignore the banner aren’t included: added
tasso.riepIgnoraNonso: unknown whether visitors who ignore it are included
tasso.usato: Value used in the calculation: {v}, plausible between {a} and {b}.
tasso.intendi: You entered a fraction: do you mean {v}%?

esperti.interruttoreNota: Rates by device and period; absolute numbers; how sure you are about each assumption.
esperti.conteggiUsa: Use absolute numbers instead of the percentage
esperti.deviceNota: For each device: consent rate and share of the sessions you see in GA4. At least two rows are needed; they replace the percentage above. The file doesn’t contain the device, so results aren’t split by device.
esperti.periodiNota: The main rate applies from the start; from each date on, the new rate applies.
esperti.d1: Do you have the CMP’s numbers instead of a percentage?
esperti.d2: Does consent differ between mobile and desktop?
esperti.d3: Did you change the banner during the period?
esperti.aperteNota: You’ll find them in the “Consent rate” card; next to each assumption you can say how sure you are.
esperti.conteggiQuando: Your CMP tells you how many people accepted and how many didn’t, not just the percentage.
esperti.conteggiMigliora: The uncertainty on the rate becomes that of the counts (at least 1 point) instead of the 5 points of “It’s an estimate”: the session range narrows.
esperti.deviceQuando: Consent differs a lot between mobile and desktop and you know the rate for each.
esperti.deviceMigliora: In the test with 50% consent on mobile, 75% on desktop and one and a half times the visits on desktop, the session error goes from about +4% to about 0% (B16).
esperti.periodiQuando: You changed the banner or CMP during the file’s period.
esperti.periodiMigliora: It fixes the split across days; in the test with a change from 60% to 35% the totals stay correct even without declaring it (B12).

ip.gruppoIpotesi: Assumptions about visitors who don’t accept
ip.gruppoIpotesiNota: Nobody has measured them: they are reasoned values. Check them, or leave them as they are.
ip.rFreqFrase: Visitors who don’t accept make {v} visits for every visit by those who accept.
ip.rFreqAiuto: Many visitors who don’t accept are just passing through, so on average they make fewer visits each. The starting value depends on how your CMP measures the rate.
ip.rConvFrase: A visit from someone who doesn’t accept converts {v} times as often as a visit from someone who does.
ip.rConvAiuto: Google says that users who consent “typically” convert 2 to 5 times more, which means a value between 0.2 and 0.5.
ip.rConvConflitto: With real orders it would have to be about {v}.
ip.rConvConflittoNota: The range you set is {a} – {b}. What could explain it is in the results.
ip.rAov: How much they spend per order
ip.rAovFrase: Visitors who don’t accept spend {v} times as much as those who accept.
ip.rAovAiuto: There’s no strong reason to expect a difference, so it starts at 1.
ip.ricorda: Remember the assumptions on this device
ip.ricordaNota: Off by default. The link and the memory hold only answers and assumptions: never the file, orders or users.
ip.rFreqCursore: {v}: visitors who don’t accept make {v} visits for every visit by those who accept. Plausible between {a} and {b}
ip.rConvCursore: {v}: a visit from someone who doesn’t accept converts {v} times as often as one from someone who does. Plausible between {a} and {b}
ip.rAovCursore: {v}: visitors who don’t accept spend {v} times as much as those who accept. Plausible between {a} and {b}

ordini.invito: Do you have the orders from your order system for the same period? It’s the data that helps most: it narrows orders and revenue a lot.
ordini.confrontabili: Enter orders comparable with GA4: website only, without phone or in-store orders, automatic renewals or test orders. Revenue with the same definition as GA4 (tax, shipping, refunds).
ordini.pubblico: What audience does the site have?
ordini.pubblicoAiuto: Some orders escape GA4 for reasons other than consent: mostly ad blockers and browsers that block Google Analytics, far more common among technical audiences and on desktop, plus some technical errors. This answer splits the missing orders between “consent” and “other reasons”. Only orders from visitors who accepted cookies count here (or who never saw the banner because a blocker hid it): orders from visitors who declined are already “missing because of consent”.
ordini.pubblicoManca: Choose the audience type to use real orders.
ordini.server: I use server-side tagging or my own proxy
ordini.ordini_senza_transazioni: The file has no transactions in the selected period, so real orders can’t be used.
ordini.ordini_inferiori: The real orders you entered ({ordini}) are fewer than the GA4 transactions in the same period ({transazioni}). Check the period, possible duplicate transactions in GA4 or a different scope between the two systems.
ordini.scontrino_diverso: The average order value in your order system and in GA4 differ by {percento}%: revenue is probably defined differently (tax, shipping, refunds). Real revenue wasn’t used.

utenti.invito: To estimate unique users you need the total users for the period from GA4: the daily export doesn’t contain it.
utenti.campo: Total users for the whole period, from GA4
utenti.nota: Adding up each day’s users counts returning visitors several times. Use the value in the total row of your export, or read the total in GA4 (same period, without the Date dimension).
utenti.notaExport: Read from the totals row of your export, already deduplicated by GA4.
utenti.notaUtente: Total users for the whole period, entered by you.
utenti.notaNo: Your export contains the total users for the period ({v}), but you chose not to use it.
utenti.csvExport: {v}, read from the export’s totals row

ris.errore_nessuna_riga: The file has no data rows.
ris.eroe: GA4 shows you about {pct} of sessions.
ris.eroeIntervallo: Likely between {a} and {b} (8 times out of 10), if the assumptions are right.
ris.eroeAiuto: “8 times out of 10” isn’t a figure of speech: on test data with a known answer, the true value falls in this range about 8 times out of 10. It holds if the assumptions are right; if one is badly wrong, the true value can fall outside. Almost certainly (19 times out of 20) it’s between {a} and {b}.
ris.eroeAria: Share of sessions GA4 shows: about {pct}, likely between {a} and {b}
ris.eroeTransazioni: And about {pct} of transactions (between {a} and {b}): the visits you don’t see convert less, so proportionally fewer orders are missing.
ris.eroeTransazioniOrdini: And about {pct} of your real orders.
ris.utentiNo: Unique users: can’t be estimated from this file.
ris.utentiNoNota: Adding up each day’s users counts returning visitors several times. Enter the total in “Users in the period”.
ris.utentiGiornoNota: “User-days” is the sum of users for each day and channel: they aren’t distinct people. Visitors who don’t accept have no identifier, so nobody has ever counted the distinct people without consent.
ris.ordiniNota: Real orders tell you how many are missing, not why. The split between the last two depends on the audience type you chose ({pubblico}).
ris.ordiniAria: Real orders split into seen by GA4, missing because of consent and missing for other reasons
ris.transazioniConsenso: Transactions: seen + missing because of consent
ris.entrateConsenso: Revenue: seen + missing because of consent
ris.ordiniParziali: Real orders used for the period {dal} – {al}: {n}.
ris.cautela: Use this estimate with caution: you haven’t checked whether the export already contains data estimated by Google. If it does, traffic without consent is counted twice.
ris.soloConfronto: With Google’s modeling active, don’t use these numbers as totals: they are calculated on the second export (observed data only) and are for comparison only.
ris.esempio: You’re looking at fake data. The answers (Consent Mode, rate) are part of the example too.
ris.daLink: Answers and assumptions came from a link: check them before trusting the result.
ris.linkIgnorato: The link contained assumptions in an unrecognized format: they were ignored.
ris.limiti: It’s an estimate, not a measurement · it covers missing consent only, not ad blockers or technical errors
ris.incompleto: A required answer is missing: complete the “Consent Mode” and “Consent rate” cards to update the estimate.
ris.stampaNota: It’s an estimate, not a measurement: it depends on the assumptions listed below.
ris.perchePiu: {P} is the share of visitors who accept{corretto}. Visitors who accept come back more often (assumption: those who don’t accept make {r} visits for each of theirs), so they weigh more in sessions.
ris.percheMeno: {P} is the share of visitors who accept{corretto}. Here visitors who don’t accept come back more often (assumption: they make {r} visits for each one by those who accept), so the sessions of those who accept weigh less.
ris.percheCorretto: , after the correction stated in your answers
ris.percheGenerico: Why doesn’t the share of sessions match the consent rate? Visitors who accept and those who don’t come back a different number of times (the “How often they come back” assumption), so they weigh differently in sessions. With different rates by device or period the calculation combines them, and a single number can’t show it.
ris.errore_worker: The calculation code didn’t load: the page was opened without a connection, or loading was interrupted. Reload the page with the network on; after that, the estimate works offline too.
ris.utentiNoNotaTotali: You chose not to use the total users from your export: you can turn it back on in “Users in the period”.
ris.canaliIgnorati: The assumptions you received contained rates by channel: the Estimator no longer uses them, so they were ignored.

cambiato.nota: Real orders tell you how many orders are missing, not how many visits: for sessions, the consent rate is what matters.

graf.canaliAria: {m} by channel: observed and estimated total with ranges. The values are also in the table.
graf.giorniAria: {m} by day: observed and estimated total with ranges. Use the arrow keys to move between days; the values are also in the table.
graf.canaliAvviso: The split by channel is the least solid part. The total doesn’t depend on how consent is distributed across channels; the split does: it assumes similar consent in all of them. If a channel probably accepts much less than the others (for example paid social), read its figure as indicative.

solid.nonDisponibile: With real orders the sources of uncertainty offset each other and can’t be separated.
solid.rimedio_consenso: To narrow the range: a more reliable consent rate. Uploading more days doesn’t help.
solid.rimedio_frequenza: To narrow the range: knowing how often visitors who don’t accept come back (for example from a cookieless analytics tool). Uploading more days doesn’t help.
solid.rimedio_conversione: To narrow the range: enter the real orders from your order system. Uploading more days doesn’t help.
solid.rimedio_scontrino: To narrow the range: enter real orders and revenue from your order system.
solid.rimedio_rumore: To narrow the range: a longer period: there’s little data here.
solid.rimedio_ordini: To narrow it further: for sessions, a more reliable consent rate; for orders and revenue, knowing what audience the site has.
solid.eSe: What if an assumption were wrong?
solid.eSeNota: Total {m} if a single assumption moves from one end of its range to the other, with the others fixed.
solid.eSeOrdini: With real orders the assumptions are no longer independent: if one goes up, “how well they convert” goes down to stay consistent with the orders. The chart moves them one at a time, so it overstates the effect on transactions and revenue.
solid.aria: Effect of each assumption on total {m}
solid.semplice: For comparison, the simple calculation (observed ÷ consent rate) would give {v}: it ignores that visitors who don’t accept come back and convert differently.
solid.fidarsiSim: The estimate of “{m}” may vary by about ±{v} (8 times out of 10): likely between {a} and {b}.
solid.fidarsiAsim: The estimate of “{m}” may vary from −{lo} to +{hi} (8 times out of 10): likely between {a} and {b}.
solid.dipendeNota: The sources of uncertainty, most important first. The percentage is how much each one weighs on the width of the range.
solid.spiega_consenso: How reliable the number you entered is, and how your CMP calculates it.
solid.spiega_frequenza: It’s an assumption: nobody measures the visits of those who don’t accept.
solid.spiega_conversione: It’s an assumption: without real orders nobody measures it.
solid.spiega_scontrino: It’s an assumption: without real revenue nobody measures it.
solid.spiega_rumore: With few days or small channels the numbers fluctuate.
solid.consiglioConsenso: To make it more reliable: check in your CMP how it’s calculated (per visitor or per banner, with or without visitors who ignore the banner); if you have the absolute numbers of acceptances and non-acceptances, enter them in expert settings. Uploading more days doesn’t help.
solid.eSeCentrale: Current estimate: ≈ {v}. Each box moves a single assumption to the ends of its plausible range, with the others fixed.

confronto.nota: How much Google’s modeling added to the observed data alone, and how much this estimator would have added.
confronto.colStrumento: Addition estimated by the estimator (19 times out of 20)
confronto.avvertenza: A result “outside the range” doesn’t tell you who is right: the two methods use different information. If Google’s addition is negative or zero, check that both exports cover the same period.

esporta.linkCopiato: Link copied. It holds only answers and assumptions: never the file, orders or users.
esporta.nota: CSV and PDF are created in this tab. They always list the assumptions used and how many are defaults.
esporta.csvNotaTesto: Estimates that depend on the stated assumptions: they aren’t measured data.
esporta.noPochi: no: fewer orders are missing than the answers predict
esporta.noTroppi: no: more orders are missing than the answers predict

tour.t1: The answers (Consent Mode Basic, 60% rate) belong to the example too, not to you. With your own file you’ll give them yourself, and nothing will be preset.
tour.t2: GA4 shows only part of the sessions. The range tells you how far to trust it: “likely between…” holds 8 times out of 10, if the assumptions are right.
tour.t3: Three values nobody has measured. Try moving one: the results change right away. Until you confirm them they stay marked “Default”.
tour.t4: This is the data that helps most. Enter the orders from the fake order system and watch the transactions range narrow.
tour.t5: You can download the results, copy a link with the assumptions, or upload your own file.

schema.catenaAria: Observed sessions, times the ratio of declines to acceptances, times how often they come back, give the missing sessions; times the conversion rate and how well they convert, they give the missing conversions.
schema.perConversione: × conversion rate × how well they convert
schema.imbutoAria: Of a hundred visitors, sixty accept and GA4 sees them; twenty-six decline and fourteen ignore the banner: GA4 sees neither group.
schema.sessAria: Ten visitors in rows: six accept and make three visits each, four don’t accept and make two visits each. 60% of visitors produce 69% of sessions.
schema.alberoAria: Three questions: Consent Mode Basic leads to the estimate; Advanced with a reporting identity other than “Blended” leads to the estimate; Advanced, “Blended” and the “Including” icon lead to not adjusting; any “I don’t know” leads to an estimate with caution.
schema.alberoCautela: “I don’t know” to a question: estimate with caution
schema.ventaglioAria: The calculation is repeated thousands of times with different assumptions; the results form a curve. The central 80% is the “8 times out of 10” range, the central 95% is “19 times out of 20”.
schema.ordiniAria: Real orders split into seen by GA4, missing because of consent and missing for other reasons. The boundary between the last two isn’t known precisely.
schema.ordiniReali: Real orders from your order system
schema.ordiniConfine: this boundary depends on the audience type
schema.visiteOrdiniTitolo: A hundred visits as dashes: 69 solid ones are counted, 31 dashed ones are without consent. Below, the orders: 9 among the counted visits, about 2 among those without consent.
schema.visiteOrdiniNota: Same example: 100 visits, 60% consent rate. Visitors who don’t accept convert about 0.4 times as often as those who accept.
schema.sessDidascalia: 6 visitors out of 10 accept, 18 sessions out of 26 are counted (69%)

val.didascalia: How many times out of 100 the true value falls in the “8 out of 10” / “19 out of 20” range. It should be close to 80 / 95.
val.didascaliaErrore: Median error of the central estimate on the total: sessions / transactions.
val.repliche: {n} runs per scenario, {sim} simulations per estimate.

scenario.B8b: True “how well they convert” 0.15, with real orders
scenario.B9: Consent very different across channels (30% to 85%)

scenario.B11b: Rate excluding visitors who ignore the banner, declared as such

scenario.B13b: Real orders, true other losses 20%, audience declared “consumer”

scenario.B15b: 12% ad blockers who decline more often, with real orders

griglia.titolo: A hundred visits: those GA4 counts and those without consent
griglia.semplice: GA4 sees {p} visits out of 100, {m0} are missing.
griglia.stima: GA4 sees about {c} visits out of 100 (likely between {a} and {b}), about {m} are missing.

vetrina.nota: Sample data (fake), calculated with the estimator
vetrina.v1: How much of your sessions GA4 shows you, with the “likely between…” range and its condition written next to it.
vetrina.v2: Sessions, transactions, revenue and key events by channel and day by day, with a warning where the estimate is less solid.
vetrina.v3: Which assumption weighs most and how the total would change if it were wrong: you know which data is worth getting.
vetrina.v4: CSV and PDF created in your browser, always with the list of assumptions used; a link to share only the assumptions.
vetrina.csvTitolo: The CSV, first rows and assumptions
vetrina.omesse: … {n} more rows by channel and by day …
vetrina.pdf: PDF with header, date and assumptions

risolve.titolo: Dividing by the consent rate isn’t enough.
risolve.lead: Two separate effects shift the count. The example is the same across the page: 100 visits, a 60% consent rate, visitors who accept make 3 visits and those who don’t make 2.
risolve.aTitolo: Visitors who accept come back more often
risolve.aEvidenza: 6 visitors out of 10 accept, but GA4 counts 18 sessions out of 26.
risolve.aRiga: That’s why the share of sessions you see is higher than the consent rate.
risolve.aAria: Ten visitors: six accept and make three visits each, all counted by GA4; four don’t accept and make two visits each, which GA4 doesn’t see. GA4 counts 18 sessions out of 26.
risolve.bTitolo: Visitors who don’t accept buy less
risolve.bEvidenza: The missing visits hold about 2 orders, not 4.
risolve.bRiga: Out of 100 visits GA4 counts 69, with 9 orders. The 31 without consent convert about 0.4 times as often.
risolve.bAria: A hundred visits as dashes: 69 counted, 31 without consent. Below, the orders: 9 among the counted visits, about 2 among those without consent.
risolve.cFrase: In the example the simple calculation overestimates sessions by 15% and orders by about 40%. Uncounted accounts for both effects and tells you how uncertain the estimate is.
risolve.cAria: Comparison in the example. Sessions: the simple calculation gives 115, in the example there are 100 (69 counted and 31 not seen). Orders: the simple calculation gives 15, in the example there are about 11 (9 counted and about 2 not seen).

conti.titoloPochi: Fewer orders are missing than your answers predict
conti.titoloTroppi: More orders are missing than your answers predict
conti.intro: Your order system tells you how many orders GA4 didn’t record. That’s useful: probably one answer, or one of the figures you entered, doesn’t describe the site well.
conti.realiDa: ({o} in your order system − {t} in GA4)
conti.altreSpiega: Other causes: orders GA4 loses even with consent, for example to ad blockers, payments through an external service the customer doesn’t return from, errors in the purchase tag. How many there are depends on your answer about the audience.
conti.aria: Comparison of missing orders. {n} orders are actually missing: {o} in your order system minus {t} in GA4. Your answers predict about {p}: about {c} from consent and about {a} from other causes.
conti.pubblico: Your answer about the audience. With which answer the numbers would add up:
conti.sceglila: Choose it only if it really matches the site.
conti.nessuna: The type of audience alone can’t explain it: check the points below.
conti.altriPunti: Other points to check (these can’t be calculated):
conti.periodo: The order period: do the orders cover the same days as the file?
conti.perimetro: The scope: do your order system and GA4 count the same orders? For example phone or in-store orders, automatic renewals, other sites.
conti.tassoPochi: The consent rate: it may be higher than the one you entered.
conti.tassoTroppi: The consent rate: it may be lower than the one you entered, or not include visitors who ignore the banner.
conti.doppie: Transactions counted twice in GA4: for example when the confirmation page is reloaded. Compare transaction IDs with those in your order system.
conti.stato: Until the numbers add up, orders and revenue are estimated without real orders. Sessions and users don’t change.
conti.tecnico: With these answers, for the numbers to add up the “how well they convert” assumption would have to be about {v} (visitors who don’t accept would convert {v} times as often as those who accept), outside the plausible range you set ({a} – {b}). That’s why real orders aren’t used.
